utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 17th of February 2010. I would like to greet everyone in the courtroom, the counsel, the accused, Mr. Scott, everyone from the OTP, as well as everybody else helping us in the courtroom. I would also like to apologise for the delay in starting this session. It is my fault, but in a previous hearing that I was chairing the Prosecutor wanted to take the floor for an administrative issue, and unfortunately we finished late. So I would like to apologise for that. I believe that Mr. Kovacic has something to say, so I'll give him the floor immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me the floor. Good afternoon to Your Honours and everybody else in the courtroom. Your Honours, I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber to grant me an extension of the dead-line for submitting the various submissions and motions with respect to two rulings made by this Trial Chamber; first of all, in respect of the Chamber decision of the 16th of February, 2010, which -- and that is the decision concerning Defence witness under 92 bis. I'd like to remind you that the decision is 20 pages' long, and I'd also like to remind you that it was made two and a half months after all the motions were submitted, the motion response, and motion replies, and the Trial Chamber obviously needed a lot of time to get through that job, which is no mean task. As you know, we're a small team with small resources, and when looking through it we saw some technical errors. We noticed some. We didn't see whether they were more important or not, but we do think that we'll need at least until the end of next week or, let me say, a Monday week - not this Monday but the following Monday - to compile a reasonable request for a re-examination of individual decisions, or parts of decisions, or decisions on certain documents, or alternatively we should like to lodge an appeal. Now, as far as the other ruling is concerned, and it was the ruling of the Trial Chamber of the 15th of February and was filed on the same day, there, too -- I apologise. I must take a moment. I made a mistake. In the first motion about 92 bis witnesses, there's no question of reconsideration. We'd just like to have leave for a certification for leave to appeal. So we'd like to ask for certification to appeal. And as I said, it was a 20-page-long ruling. We, of course, understand the dispositions in it, and we have a working translation from the French, of course, as French is the official language or one of the official languages. We did, nonetheless, wish to make sure we understood the Trial Chamber's reasoning in its entirety and fully, so perhaps the Trial Chamber could make a request that we receive a translation as soon as possible and that the dead-line starts running after we receive an English translation or, anyway, to be given a dead-line until Monday week, not this Monday but the following Monday. So that's what I wanted to say with respect to the 92 bis witnesses. Now, as far as the 15th of February decision is concerned, which relates to the adoption of exhibits used during General Praljak's testimony, I'd first of all like to remind you that it concerns 255 documents in all. The Trial Chamber, once again, needed considerable time to go through all those documents, and of course we will need quite a lot of time to go through them ourselves. Up until now, we have found that there are several exhibits which justify a request for re-examination and reconsideration, and this relates to technical errors, figures, or whether the document was on the 65 ter list or not, and similar things, and also requires a lot of time to go through everything and check it all. And with respect to that ruling, too, we would also like to ask, as I said earlier on, certification to appeal, and I'm sure you'll understand that for both these motions, we require a little more time than just seven days. And, therefore, I consider that in conformity with Rule 127, there is good cause for us to make that request. If you wish to hear the details, I'll be happy to give you them. I'll tell you of the team we have and the difficulties that we're facing because one of our important members will not be available until the 3rd of March. But, anyway, for both those motions we should like to be given more time, at least until the Monday week, especially for the 92 bis decision, and we'd like to have the seven-day dead-line start running from the day that we receive the English translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a point of clarification before the Chamber confers. The 92 bis decision or ruling is a 20-page document, and my opinion is of 6 pages. So it will be 26 pages altogether, so I don't know how long it will take for this translation to be made. But you basically want two weeks once you receive the translation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't wish to be immodest. I'm trying to be rational with the use of time. My request -- well, I have one request and an alternative request. The first request would be a week after we have received the English translation. If that seems to be too long, then, regardless -- as I said, one week after we receive the English translation. If that seems too long to you or if the English translation will take too much time, then we could live with the next request if you give us time until Monday fortnight; so not the coming Monday, but the Monday after that. Yes, I apologise, but I seem to have lost my notebook where I noted down the exact dates of that particular Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has unanimously deliberated and grants the Praljak Defence one week to do their submissions, their original submissions, and that is going to be starting from the time they receive the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And the Monday I mean is the 1st of March. I've just looked it up. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another administrative issue. I wanted to advise the Stojic Defence, who drew my attention on the two lists that I have said regarding the documents, in fact, three documents are not going to be used. And I'm going to give the numbers, because those documents have not been admitted. P00810 - it was actually the Stojic Defence that contacted me - P01336, and P02646. Those three documents were signed by Mr. Stojic, and those documents will not be put forward to General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. I'd just like to thank Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll proceed, but I had a follow-up question, because I'm rather slow and I think through things overnight. And I remembered an answer made by General Petkovic, and I wanted to double-check it, because it has legal consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, when you left on the Friday before the 9th of May -- Sunday was the 9th of May, Saturday was the 8th, so Friday was the 7th, so when you left for Split on the 7th of May to spend the weekend there, Split was in a foreign country at the time, because this was the Republic of Croatia. When you left your position, because you were the chief of staff of the HVO, I was wondering whether, either verbally or in written form, you delegated your authority to one of your second-in-command, or another officer, or did you do nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, every time, for justified reasons, I happened to be absent from the Main Staff for a day or two; maybe longer sometimes. Then, in the log-book that we had for coming tasks, for future tasks, a log-book where we recorded the assignments, we would make an entry with tasks and assignments that are expected over those one, two, or several days, so that people knew what to focus on. And every duty officer and the duty team on duty at that time knew that on such and such a day, these were the assignments; number 1, number 2, number 3, and so on. So that every team had to know this, and that is standard practice in every army, including the HVO. So that was everybody's duty at all levels; brigade commander, up and down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, General. But I also had duty tasks at a very high level, and I know what it means to find out who is going to replace whom. But when you said that you left it in a log-book for the person on duty, what had to be done, I was wondering, in case a need arised [as interpreted] -- in case there was a need, did anyone know who they would have to speak to? And given that you were in the Republic of Croatia, would you be the person that would be contacted or would it be somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the practice was that in addition to the people, there was an operative team made up of five or six people who would be at home, on duty at home, and if need be they would be called up. And in a document that Mr. Praljak had, we changed all that, and we kept the whole operative team in the Main Staff at headquarters. Otherwise, in addition to the three or four people who were on duty, people were on duty at home, too, and they knew that if anything was needed, they would be called up, which would mean a team of seven or eight men at headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please listen carefully, because my question is very important, and I don't waste my time asking questions that are not important. So listen carefully. You are in Split. Let's assume for a moment that we have a town where there is some members of the HVO, and there's a major offensive from the ABiH, and you were not expecting such an offensive. So in a matter of minutes your soldiers are out of sorts and you need immediate back-up, and you are busy buying your tomatoes on a market-place and you cannot be contacted. Who will make a decision to send a message to all -- or to send an order to all commanders of operative zones to strengthen all units that are in trouble, because you're not there, you're in Split, and you're busy buying your tomatoes, so who will send this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if that kind of information is received in the Main Staff, that there is some danger in a certain part, then the team on duty has the responsibility of warning the command of the operative zone and say, Gather up the operative zone team and deal with the situation, take command of the situation. And with that, the other people would come in that were on this what we called operative duty, that is to say, duty at home. So the team at headquarters and the team at home activates all the subordinate units, bring them up to strength, gather them together, and that was the standard practice. That was how these people were alerted and called in, and that was how the normal chain of command functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I understand, when you were in Split on the 7th, 8th, and 9th of May before you went back, it was for the officers on duty to manage any problem. Why was I asking you this? Well, I wanted to double-check, because the Appeals Chamber, in a recent decision of the 12th of November, 2009, states the following, and I'm going to quote. It's not going to be very long. It has to do with the Dragomir Milosevic case. So listen carefully: "The Appeals Chamber would like to recall that when Dragomir Milosevic was sent to hospital in Belgrade, it was his chief of staff, Cedomir Sladojev, who was in charge of the SRK Command in Sarajevo, and this person was giving the orders instead of the commander." So the Appeals Chamber concludes that even if Dragomir Milosevic had officially retained his rank and his function, the authority on the ground was dealt with by the person that was the deputy on the ground. This is why I asked the question. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, to you, the Prosecution, you, General, and everybody else in the courtroom. Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, may I just draw your attention to something with respect to your -- what you last said on the previous page, line 15. General Petkovic did not say that on the 9th of May, he was in Split. General Petkovic said that on the 7th of May, he went to Split, and that he returned to Mostar on the 9th of May, in the early afternoon. Just to avoid any misunderstanding on that score later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, today we're going to deal with the 30th of June, 1993. To start off with, tell us this, please: If you told us that in June 1993 the BH Army took control of Travnik and Kakanj, and if we know that on the 30th of June it took control of the area north of East Mostar, towards Jablanica, on the left bank of the Neretva River, then where is the difference between taking control of Travnik and Kakanj, for example, and taking control of this area north of Eastern Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as the area that the BH Army took control of, there's no difference. But there is a difference in the grouping of forces carrying out that assignment, because in April it was the BH Army forces that took Kakanj and Travnik, whereas in Mostar our own Muslims, Muslims within the HVO, committed a treacherous act, and then they went on to take control of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I correct the transcript. In line 24, it says that the general spoke about April, but we're talking about taking control of Kakanj and Travnik in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember saying "April." I think I said "June."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just correcting the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Talking about dates, I have to come back to something which happened a bit earlier. Mr. Petkovic, on the morning of the 9th May, where did you awake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 9th of May, in the morning, I woke up in Mr. Stojic's apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And where was that; in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, in Citluk, where his parents lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you left Split on the -- sometime when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I arrived at the Stojic family's house in the evening hours of the 8th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Another additional question. Which route did you take with Mr. Stojic on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left for the Operative Zone in North-West Herzegovina. It was our intention to arrive at Prozor, at Colonel Siljeg's command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us return to the 30th of June. If I understood you correctly, the difference between this event and the previous events is the fact that the ABiH had taken the area north of East Mostar in co-operation with the Muslim soldiers of the HVO. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, before that was there a single incident in which the Muslim soldiers of the HVO turned their weapons on their Croatian colleagues in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there have been no such incidents. But some of them simply left the HVO after the 9th of May, but did not engage in any combat activities against HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was your reaction and that of the other HVO commanders once you understood that part of the area was lost due to this act committed by the Muslim HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were afraid that this would trigger a chain reaction throughout the HVO units that had a significant share of Muslim soldiers in their ranks, so we were a little short of panic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In South-East Herzegovina, what was the average number of Muslims in the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Brigades of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The average share was about 30 to 35 per cent in these three brigades. It changed, of course, with -- or, rather, depending on whether they grew stronger or weaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was this relevant for you, as chief of Main Staff, with regard to security?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How was it relevant?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the risk that the entire area to the east and south of Mostar, even including the western part of Mostar, might be lost for the HVO in that manner, because the worst thing that could happen to an army is a rebellion in its own ranks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the following set of documents, the first one being P3019. This is your order dated the 30th of June, and you sent it to the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina. What has been the focus of our interest and will remain so is item 8 of this order, where you say that: "In the units where there are soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, these are to be isolated and disarmed." And you also say: "In places where there is a Muslim population, all able-bodied Muslim men should be isolated." And it goes on to say that: "Women and children should be left in their houses and apartments." I correct the document reference. It is document P3019. Tell us, General, is this your order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On this 30th of June, in the morning, when you learned what was going on in the area north-east of Mostar, and when you learned of the treason of the Muslim HVO soldiers, did you speak to anybody about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first stayed for about two hours in the Command of the OZ South-East Herzegovina to try to establish with them who was where at that given moment, so it took us about two hours, from 7.00 to 9.00, because we wanted to get -- to have a real picture of what was going on. Once we were sure how things really worked, I received a phone call from Mr. Boban. At 9.00, once the information had been collected, I returned to the Main Staff, and I spoke to Mr. Boban. I presented the information that was presented to me at the OZ to him. I listened to everybody who was able to give any information, and I also used a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, can you reproduce your conversation with Boban as faithfully as possible? What exactly did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once he heard what I had to say, he said that it did differ from what he had heard before. I suppose that, among others, he also spoke to the mayor of Mostar, so that information may be different from that information which the army had. He asked me, General, you were convincing us that you can rely on your soldiers of Muslim ethnicity. Any warnings to the effect that this was risky was rejected by you -- were rejected? And he asked me what I was planning to do with my Muslims, as he put it, and I said, Well, we'll wait a bit longer, and then we'll assess the situation and see how it develops. At that moment, he said to me, You know, General, from this moment on, you must start disarming all these people you have in your units, if it isn't too late already. Do you have any idea what's happening south of Mostar? As far as I can tell and judging what happened, we will not only lose the entire area south of Mostar, and also put Croatia in jeopardy, because you know that it is their wish to reach the coast, because they want to take not only Neum, they also want the port of Ploce.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you understand that to mean or that to be an order of your supreme commander, or did you take that to be a piece of advice from a co-worker?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the conversation continued, and we tried to find the best ways and means of disarming the soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, and everybody else who could be a threat for the HVO should be isolated. To me, that was an order which I included in my order in this item that has two components. Around 11.00 or 12.00, I started drafting that order, once I received information from the OZ, because I wanted them to provide information about the positions that we could take.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When your supreme commander issued you this order to disarm soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, did you consider that to be a legal or an illegal order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a legal order, and it would be such in any army in the whole world. You must take care of a rebellion in your ranks in whichever way you think appropriate, and disarming is one such way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From the aspect of security, the security of the HVO, did you consider this order of your commander-in-chief justified?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you spoke to the supreme commander, did you mention the number of Muslim soldiers of the HVO and able-bodied Muslim men that would be affected by this isolation campaign?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me about the number of Muslim soldiers who had defected to the ABiH and how many were left in our units. He also wanted to know how many collaborators, or, that is, able-bodied men that were left who could join the ranks of the ABiH. Knowing the approximate number of men, and taking into consideration that you certainly cannot disarm each and every one, the estimate we came up with was 2.500 to 3.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your conversation with the supreme commander of the HVO, did you mention the facilities of where these isolated Muslim HVO soldiers and able-bodied Muslim men could find accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that the HVO had facilities that can put up this number of men and that it was up to the army to disarm these men in the safest manner, and everybody else was somebody -- oh, sorry, everything else was for someone else to take care of.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, how did you feel when you wrote this order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt cheated and double-crossed, because we were accepting a large number of Muslim men into the HVO. On the other hand, whenever anything happened outside of Mostar, where there were the most Muslims in the ranks of the HVO, I tried to make it clear to my counterparts in the ABiH that we can function this way and do everything with this composition of our forces. And I tried to convince my colleague, Mr. Halilovic, that this was the right way and that we should both go about our work in this manner. In such a situation, it wasn't easy to accept the fact that you were backing up the policy of accepting people in the HVO and then they turned against you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You're saying it wasn't easy, General. But how do you feel? That's what I wanted to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I felt shattered, completely shattered. Everything I had hoped for was simply falling apart, and I simply couldn't -- I couldn't come by. And it wasn't easy to pass such a decision, and I feared that there could have been losses due to fighting in the process of disarming. However, that didn't happen, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you were drafting this order to isolate able-bodied Muslim men, how did you treat those people? At that moment, what was their status to you, as an HVO man?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Able-bodied Muslim men, to my mind at that moment, were only -- could only be members of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you, personally, consider those able-bodied Muslim men prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would come under that category.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, at the point that you isolate Muslim soldiers from the HVO, regardless of the reasons for that, in your opinion, does that soldier retain the status of HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully. There's no difference between him and somebody else whom we detained because he refused to take up his position. So, yes, he does retain his status as an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this order, General, we see that the you say that the women and children should be left in their homes and not touched. What was your position on the protection of civilians, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position was that this category was not a threat to security in any way, and, therefore, that it was quite understandable and reasonable that they should be left to remain in their houses, where they lived, regardless of what people called total national defence. But as far as I was concerned, this category, women, children and the elderly, did not present a threat; that is to say, all those who weren't able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the end of this document, General, we see that your order was sent to the South-East Herzegovina Operations Zone and that the command of that operations zone sent it on to the 2nd and 3rd HVO Brigades. He forwarded it to them. Now, to the best of your knowledge, General, Miljenko Lasic, did he forward your order to the 1st HVO Brigade as well?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not look at my order, the one that reached Miljenko Lasic, so I didn't know what he did at that time, but I did know that the 1st Brigade started acting upon the order. So if it didn't receive the order in this form, quite obviously it did receive it in another form, in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not my intention to pursue questions on this document, so if you would like to ask the general anything on it, perhaps this is the opportune moment. If not, we can move on. General, let's look at the next document, which is 4D480.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, is that one of your documents?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, did you personally send a document with these contents to somebody else, or did you just send it to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document went to the Defence Department, and I think late in the afternoon the same contents and the same document was sent out I don't know whether to all operative zones or just to Central Bosnia, because they called to see what was happening with relation to the events in Mostar, so we -- and they asked that the same document be sent to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From this document - we've already looked at it in this courtroom, but, anyway - in the penultimate paragraph we see that you say that in all the units, measures had been taken to remove Muslims from the HVO. Now, my question to you is this: Did you inform the supreme commander of your order and of the measures of isolation to be taken for Muslim soldiers in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did inform him on that same day, because we had further contacts by night-time, and I told him that I had taken these measures and that probably the very next day they would start acting upon them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's look at the next document, which is P3175, General. 3175 is the document number, and it's under seal. It's a report from the European Monitors, a daily report, with Nedjeljko Obradovic's statements and reports for the 4th of July, and he speaks about the isolation of Muslim soldiers within the HVO because of a possible threat from inside, and he also speaks about the isolation or, rather, arrest of Muslim men aged between 18 and 60. Now, my question to you, General, is: Did the HVO in any way hide from the internationals that they had undertaken to isolate Muslim soldiers in the HVO and Muslims who were able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never kept that secret. They came to see Obradovic, he received them, and I can see that he told them about the situation and all the measures that had been taken. And this covers two pages in that particular report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, General. P3427 is the number. Once again, it is under seal. It is another European Monitors' report, dated the 13th of July, 1993, and they are conveying the statement made by Kresimir Zubak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, this document is of international nature, and it relates to a talk Colonel Obradovic had with the person who will later write the report, or maybe with someone else. We don't know. Whatever the case, he says on July 4th, and it's an important date, on July 4th the HVO started an operation to remove the Muslim men from the forces; i.e., about 25 per cent of the troops were removed from the HVO forces. And it is written here, black and white, that these people were arrested, and that they were between 18 and 60. So nothing is hidden here. Now, when Colonel Obradovic stated this, did he say this with your authorisation or with Mate Boban's authorisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we talked to the commanders and said that it would be a good thing to supply information to the internationals, whether it be the Observer Mission, the Monitors, UNPROFOR or whoever, because they were there on assignment and they asked us to help them carry out their assignment. So they had to come and visit our units, and you couldn't say, Colonel Obradovic is not going to say anything, or, You go and see Petkovic or somebody else and they'll tell you all about it. So we did allow them, at their request, to be given basic information without entering into any political or other explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Among the 11.000 documents we have been presented with, we saw some documents where the HVO sometimes made public announcements. So why is it that in this very specific case on June 30th, in the morning, it wasn't envisaged to send out a press release stating, for example, that: "The HVO this morning, between 6.00 and 7.00 a.m., disarmed a number of soldiers from HVO units for security reasons, given the events unfolding in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," something all these lines? I mean, I'm improvising here, but something of that flavour. Why wasn't it done? Then it would have been perfectly transparent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now whether in the form that you have presented here, but, anyway, on the 30th of June, in the course of the day, a statement was issued, and we've seen it here several times in the courtroom. And this was the statement issued by the authorities of the HVO, and it was made public, it was a public statement. And we looked at that document here in the courtroom a number of times. So there was a statement on the 30th about everything that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Ms. Alaburic will give us the number of the press release. Please proceed, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, we will certainly find the number of that press release. We've seen it many times in the courtroom, and I'm sure you'll remember it once we see it. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document, General, is P3427, once again the Observer Mission, and we were talking about Kresimir Zubak, who says that it was necessary to arrest the Muslim fighters within the HVO because they led a rebellion. And then in continuation, he says that the HVO will try and exchange them or do something else with them. Anyway, General, to the best of your knowledge, did the leadership of Herceg-Bosna do its best to see that the problem of isolating soldiers and able-bodied men be solved in co-operation with the international community?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, they did try and resolve the problem with the internationals, and they contacted them straight away so that no level was left out and nothing was kept secret from any level; quite the contrary, assistance was sought, especially humanitarian aid and assistance and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the next three documents that we have prepared we're going to have to deal with very briefly because our time is running out. Anyway, General, they show that you did have knowledge about the BH Army plans to take control of the area south of Jablanica, in the direction of Mostar, and further on towards the sea. And the documents are 4D948 and 4D702. You're familiar with those documents General, so tell us now, please: Did you really have knowledge of those BH Army plans, and did you take them seriously and consider the possible axes of attack by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our knowledge was that we followed the developments in the BH Army and its offensive in Central Bosnia and in the Konjic-Jablanica areas, and we expected a further attack or movements on the part of the BH Army towards Mostar. And that is why we attempted to take certain measures to prevent that, so these are measures out of caution. Now, this other document is a letter to UNPROFOR representatives, where I wrote to Mr. Walgren, who was commander-in-chief of all the UN peace forces for ex-Yugoslavia, and to General Philippe Morillon. I wrote to them about what had happened on the 30th, but I also say that several days before that, in talking to them, I informed them that we envisage that something could happen. But I never thought that it would happen in this shape or form, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before we continue with General Petkovic's testimony, let me just say that the document we just mentioned is a statement with respect to the events of the 30th of June, is document P3038. 3038 is the number of the statement, press release.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm going to show you a series of documents, seven in all, and after that I'm going to ask you a question related to those documents. The first document is 4D469. It is an official note from Ivica Kraljevic, dated March 1993, in which he notes that pressure was being exerted on Muslims in HVO and MUP units to leave those same units. And if they failed to do so, then those Muslims are being threatened with a physical liquidation or the burning of their houses. The next document, 2D288, is a document from the Security Administration of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of BH, Fikret Muslimovic, who, in mid-April 1993, is making the following assessments: He says that: "It is realistic to expect further escalation in relations, and an all-out confrontation between the BH Army and the HVO." And then he goes on to state and he says: "It is essential that all the Muslims should be pacified as much as possible, Muslims who are in the HVO, and to prevail and see that they leave the HVO and go to the BH Army." Now, the next document, 4D33, is a document once again from the security organ of a brigade within the 4th Corps of the BH Army. Once again, the date is mid-April 1993. And among other things, it says, and I quote, that: "All Muslims, members of the HVO, should be called to take the side of their people," to stand on the side of their nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it is only a technical question. Did you mention the next document, 4D33, because I do not see it here, but it may be my fault. So then if you could clarify which document you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to 4D33, which should be in your binder, and I'm adhering to the order in the binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is 4D34. The same author, the chief of security in the 4th Corps brigade two days later on the 18th of April. He also proposes security measures, and among other, I quote: "... to establish co-operation with our fighters in the HVO and tell them of the seriousness of the situation." Now, the next document is 4D35; a brigade of the 4th Corps, on the 18th of April, 1993. The commander is Bajro Pizovic, and among other things, he says that: "The Organ for Morale," IPD, "and Religious Affairs should devise a plan for information to the Muslim soldiers who are in the units of Capljina and Stolac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. I was of the opinion that we were dealing with the events of 30 June. Is that still the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are dealing with the events of the 30th of June, but I'm trying to show you the defence and security reasons for which the measure was taken to isolate the Muslims from the HVO. And what I wish to show you on this occasion is that a series of BH Army documents talk about the systemic way in which the BH Army acted towards the Muslims in the HVO, to have them tie in with the HVO Muslims, and I want to show you and prove that what actually happened on the 30th of June, 1993, is a consequence of the long-term plan that Bosnia-Herzegovina had and systemic work to try and win over the Muslims from the HVO to the side of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right, thank you. I fully understand that. I was just impressed by the fact that it is two and a half months, practically, before the main event. Thank you. Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we showed a document for 1992 because we wanted to show that this was a plan of the ABiH which was being systematically implemented for months, and I only focused on a few documents I consider most important.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We're done with this document, General. The next one is 4D473. It is also issued by Bajro Pizovic and dated the 18th of April, 1993. He communicates with the commander of the 1st HVO Brigade, and he says, I quote: "You know very well that a large number of Muslim soldiers are in your formations, and they are Muslims and belong to this people, so it wouldn't be good if the organisation and establishment of your units were to be disrupted." And the next document is 4D36. It's a report of the commander of the 4th Corps, Mr. Arif Pasalic, in which he, on the 2nd of May, 1993, among others, reports that: "We linked up with our men in the HVO." And then he said that the men from the Capljina HVO have the task of taking Tasovcici village and the bridge in Capljina in order to prevent troops from coming in from the direction of Metkovic; also, that they had assigned the task to seize the town of Stolac with "our people in the HVO." Now, General, we have seen reports of the SIS and other bodies that controlled the security situation due to the large number of Muslim soldiers in the HVO. Did you at the Main Staff have information about such plans of the ABiH and their efforts to link up with the Muslim soldiers in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have some information, but at that time, when these drastic things were going on, we didn't have such information -- information about that. Many activities in the brigades showed that this was a matter that was being dealt with. We did have reports that some soldiers hid their weapons and reported them stolen, or that they reported they had run out of ammunition, although there was no fighting in that area for days. We hoped that all these would stop some day, but there was more and more of that. And what's worse, all this originated from the very top of the ABiH; that is, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Up until the 30th of June, 1993, did you, personally, or any other HVO commander, launch any action against HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no such action was taken against HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, except for measures that applied to everybody who failed to show up at the front-line, was facing sanctions, irrespective of their ethnicity. So there was no specific action targeted at HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you remember, we analysed some reports from the 2nd and 3rd Brigades with Witness Radmilo Jasak about how Muslim HVO soldiers were to be treated. What was the position of the brigade commanders? Did they want to keep the soldiers of Muslim ethnicity in their units?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders certainly wanted them to stay, but whoever asked to be discharged from the HVO would be issued a regular document about the end of his service in the HVO, once he had returned his weapons and other equipment that was issued to him, and after that he was supposed to report to the Defence Secretariat, but they -- and then they could go to the ABiH, or somebody may have remained passive or joined their families in Croatia or whoever. But whoever applied for that would be invited to an interview, where he would be asked about his reasons, but they would be let go. And they would also be able to return if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that you agreed with General Praljak's assessment that on that 30th of June, an all-out war broke out between the HVO and the ABiH in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell us now, in a situation of all-out war, were you the right man in the right place at the right time, as chief of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is for somebody else to say. All-out war may require somebody else who is much fiercer, much more determined, energetic, who wouldn't have a soft side for some things, somebody who would -- whose moves would be more energetic and the like. But it isn't for me to assess myself; it's for others to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're done with this chapter. If you have no questions, I can continue. It seems that there are no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I must disappoint. Excuse me. Mr. Petkovic, I'm not sure whether you can answer these questions, but I would like to have a bit more concrete picture of some of these events, of what actually happened. I would like to have a film in my head so that I can really imagine the scenes. The first moment is: How did the rebellion of the Muslims start? Did they wake up in barracks, and shot their neighbours who were still in bed? Apparently, at some places they were out at 3.00 in the night, and then were they -- were they already assembled and organised in previously-prepared Muslim units, or did they meet ad hoc, did they sneak out? Do you have any idea of what actually specifically happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, north of Mostar, the area that we're speaking about, starting from the barracks and all of Bijelo Polje, up until the front-line facing the VRS, in providing logistics to these positions there may have been a 50:50 ratio. There was a battalion which was predominantly Muslim and another which was predominantly Croat. They were battalions established based on the local principle, so they were made up of locals. According to the statements of the persons who experienced that personally, they said that people were forced to give up their weapons at gunpoint. And the barracks is an interesting example. I believe that there were four or five sentries, and one guard would walk the line and reach the neighbouring sentry point, and that's how the entire barracks actually fell or was taken. At the level of the brigade, the HVO was totally surprised, and some 80 or 90 HVO soldiers, too, crossed the Neretva River and get away. The only part of Bijelo Polje where they were unsuccessful was a place that we call "the nun's house." The command of the battalion was there, and the majority there were Croats. Some were able to escape and pass on the information about the events, and that was the first information that we received. We only learned later that two or three hours after the beginning of the events, the command of the OZ was informed. The command of the brigade was blocked, the communications centre, and the barracks where the Muslims were the majority. Only the battalion next to the nun's house still had communication with us, and that's where we got our information from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm trying to mike in. You signed so that it would make a break and I would not have to interrupt you, because this is a bit lengthy, and I may want to come back to something that is a bit further up already in the transcript. You said that some battalions were predominantly manned by Muslim soldiers. Would the commander of such a battalion and staff also be predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the 1st Battalion or the 2nd, because the battalions were manned with the inhabitants of a certain area. So if a certain area was predominantly Muslim, then the soldiers in that battalion would be mostly Muslims, and fewer would be Croats. But they worked together all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. What I did not quite understand and has not -- perhaps it's also a problem of translation, without me wanting to criticise the interpreters: On page 28, at lines 17 to 20, you talked about the barracks as being, I quote: "... an interesting example. I believe that there were four or five sentries, and one guard would walk the line and reach the neighbouring sentry point, and that's how the entire barracks actually fell or was taken." Quite frankly, this is not very -- I cannot imagine this. I see these sentries walking, and I have memories of my own military past, but never the barracks were taken then. Perhaps you could be more specific, if you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. This may not have been interpreted the best way. The barracks had four or five guards' posts manned by one guard or sentry each, and the guards were never only Muslim or only Croats. And if I'm the guard at one such post, another guard would be 300 metres away from me or so, and we would walk our lines and we would meet now and then. So measures were taken that especially at the entrance to the barracks, the guard would be disarmed in order to let the ABiH enter, and then they would go on to the other rooms and other buildings in the barracks where the people slept. And the hallways and corridors, there were the weapons, and these weapons were removed. So whoever woke up and understood what was going on tried to escape, because they didn't have weapons. Half of them swam across the Neretva with no clothes and managed to reach the other bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was the kind of account that I had in mind, and this I find absolutely helpful. The next question is a similar one, and it concerns the disarming of the Muslims. Have you been present at any such occasion when Muslim soldiers in an HVO unit were disarmed? I'm sure this did not happen in the same way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I didn't go out to any area to see how this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you do not have information on that. And the last question now is perhaps of a bit more theoretical nature. You have told us that you have disarmed Muslims who had been in HVO units, and that you had isolated them, but you also said that they continued to be soldiers of the HVO, and -- POW and members of the HVO at the same time, and this puzzles me to some extent. Did they still get money, as soldiers, from the HVO, or is it perhaps again a problem that -- or a situation where some misunderstanding has arisen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a misunderstanding. I said that disarmed HVO soldiers were not prisoners of war. They were still considered soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO. Prisoners of war were that category which belonged to the BH Army, those who actually were members of the BH Army, with everything that that entailed. They were POWs, and those who were without weapons but were potential candidates for the BH Army, which meant conscripts and so on. No HVO soldier could be a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That would have been my reaction, too. Now, the soldiers that still were HVO soldiers, we are talking of such soldiers who were also isolated? I see that you nod. You must say, Yes, so that it's in the transcript, but you don't have to say more than that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, they were isolated, isolated HVO soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the next question would be whether, according to you, this isolation could be equated to a deprivation of liberty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, "isolation" should not be taken in the classical sense of deprivation of liberty. It should have been temporarily removing these people to see what had done -- who had done what and who was responsible for what, and then who should be prosecuted further. And if not, if they weren't culpable, then they should be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have just used the term "released." And to be released, one must before be somewhat detained. You have also been very careful in saying that they should not be taken as being deprived of their liberty, in the classical sense. Simply, it is not clear to me what you want to tell us in this respect. Do you want to tell us that they were not detained and then, presumably, not released, technically, but just said goodbye, to go home, and perhaps -- if you know, it would be helpful if you could describe what the situation of these isolated HVO soldiers was, practically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those HVO members who were isolated were supposed to be in one place, under supervision, and certain measures should be taken to find the organisers from amongst them, to find who the organisers were, who the leaders were in these individual groups, and to see what each person's behaviour and conduct was, what they had done. And then on the basis of that, to take certain measures if the individuals were deemed culpable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That could apply to detention on remand, someone under an investigation. There is a certain suspicion, and then questioning and other methods perhaps are applied to see whether the suspicion is sufficiently serious to continue with the proceeding. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Then we're still back with the question: What does it mean, they were "under supervision"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was a group of people who, at a given point in time, represented a threat to security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. This goes not in the direction I am curious. I would like to know: Were they in a hotel, where they could go in and out as they pleased, or were they in a school, perhaps, where the door locked, basically, and one or several guards in front of it, or any other situation? Always, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they couldn't go out, they couldn't leave, except to go to hospital or things of that nature. They were in the facility, in the building, under supervision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. I've been a bit lengthy, but I was really interested in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll break, because it's almost 4.00. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been told that we have 44 minutes left, and I'd like to ask you, if we need extra time to complete what we intended to tell you, Your Honours, that you should allow us these few extra minutes. But I will make the request when I see we are drawing to the end of the testimony. We will be finished today, and I assume that my colleagues from the Prosecution and the Defence will be satisfied if my time is extended, because then their time will be, too, and it won't upset the plan, Your Honours that we move on tomorrow with Judge Antonetti's questions and examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, we're not going to deal with any more documents because we don't have that much time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I actually prepared myself to start immediately, so you're actually causing a problem here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There won't be a problem, Your Honours. After the break, we can move on with your questions, with your examination of General Petkovic, but I assume that if we might need an extra 10 or 15 minutes, that you will allow us that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Anyway, General, we're not going to deal with documents anymore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you need additional time, you will ask, and then the Trial Chamber will decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, Operation South, let's explain that to Their Honours in the briefest possible terms. When did you learn about the plan to launch an operation which came to be known as Operation South?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of July -- or, rather, the 5th of July, 1993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And who told you about the plan?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban called me and told me to prepare an operation like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My response was that the HVO wasn't capable of undertaking any operation and that it would be madness to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what did he say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, that he would find a team capable of carrying it out. And he was busy to come up with such a team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who was at the head of the team?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the head of the team was Brigadier Luka Dzanko.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did you in any way -- were you in any way involved in the planning of that action?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in no way was I involved in the planning of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in the command of that operation which was in Krivodol?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never joined that command, nor was I ever there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, before the beginning of the operation, itself, was a meeting held at Mate Boban's?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Boban called all the participants of the operation to attend a meeting which was held concerning the operation, itself --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the date?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date was the 13th, because the operation was supposed to start on the morning of the 13th, but there was a delay, and he called in the command to see what had caused the delay. So on the 13th of July was when it was supposed to have started, 1993. Right? I'm mixing up my dates now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did you attend the meeting at Mate Boban's?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend the meeting, and I sat to one side, listening to the others to hear what they were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, why couldn't the operation start on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that morning the BH Army infiltrated a large number of sabotage terrorist units in the Dubrava Plateau area, and so there was a lot of disturbance and a lot of fighting and a lot of casualties in the Dubravska Plateau area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, this operation, does it have anything to do with your departure from the post of the number 1 man of the Main Staff, the chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I considered that the supreme commander should have believed me and not have taken the decision to bring in a whole command team, made up of some 15 or 16 men, and to launch the operation of his own bat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did you ask the supreme commander to relieve you of your duties as chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th, in the evening, I talked to him, and I told him that I would give him 10 days to find a replacement for me and that that was proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, why did you remain in the HVO? Why didn't you leave? Why didn't you go home to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I felt the need to stay with the people that I'd spent so much time with, and I also learnt that General Praljak would be replacing me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know General Praljak, General, from before?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- well, not before the 17th or 18th of April of 1992. That's when we first met, when I arrived in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, knowing General Praljak, was it your assessment that he was a man you could co-operate with in the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did think that, because General Praljak didn't come to take up some position or anything like that, but to help the people, and it was easier to work that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General. Your Honours, if any of you has any questions about this topic, Operation South, pose them, but we'll move on. The re-subordination of the military and civilian police is the next area I'd like to deal with, and for that let's look at document P3770. We're still dealing with the second binder. It's an order from the chief of the Military Police Administration, in which it says pursuant to the order from the head of the Defence Department, part of the military police should be re-subordinated to the 3rd Brigade HVO Command. Now, does this order, General, show what should have been done when a military police unit is re-subordinated to a commander?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is standard procedure, because we're dealing with the deployment of the military police in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I'd like to say straight away that for the umpteenth time we're repeating the fact that Defence counsel is testifying, in fact, and is just asking for confirmation. Ten seconds ago, she said, General, isn't it true that the head of the Defence Department was supposed to issue an order to the chief of the military police, and then so on and so on. I think that they are statements on her part, so let's have that manner of conduct changed in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric -- Ms. Alaburic, given that you're touching on a sensitive issue, which is the military police and the relationship with the chief of staff, it's a very sensitive issue given the various interventions of Mr. Coric, I would ask you to touch upon this issue in a most neutral possible way, because as Mr. Coric rightly said so, if, in the question, you are already issuing a position, one could have problems. So please be very careful when asking those questions. General Petkovic will talk about it; I may ask questions as well; and when Mr. Coric will have some of his witnesses testifying, I'm quite sure that we will come back on this issue. So please be very cautious when you are putting those questions. Don't forget that you are doing an examination-in-chief here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just add a technical remark. I think the correct way would be if Mr. Coric would ask counsel to make such intervention, because it's really something that is the role of counsel, rather than the accused. I understand that you become impatient. That's perfectly correct. And we have granted the accused the right, personally, to ask questions, but as you are, in fact, excellently assisted by competent counsel, this is the kind of thing normally counsel should do. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you for those compliments addressed to my counsel. So on her behalf, I thank you, and I thank Ms. Alaburic, too. But I will always get up when things are repeated that should not be repeated in this courtroom, regardless of your warning. I do respect you, Your Honour. However, when it's too much, it's too much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't need to comment. I'd just like to remind you that my question was whether this document shows what should be done if a military police unit were re-subordinated to an HVO commander. That was my question. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] No, that wasn't your question. That was not your question, what your question was like. Look at the transcript. You made an observation. You didn't ask a question. Have a look at the transcript again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a criminal trial, I also take on board psychological factors. It is important for the good course of justice that everything happens as smoothly as possible, and when an accused wants to take the floor, he has to be listened to, and one shouldn't always hide behind applying rules. Rules may actually sometimes be counterproductive, and therefore you are presenting a document to the witness. Why don't you just read this document and say, This is a document with such and such a date and such and such signatory; what does this document say? And the witness will say, Well, this document talks about re-subordination, and so on and so forth. And you say, Very well, so what does that mean in military terms? And that's how we can proceed, and in that case no one can argue about anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you have said this, I really now ask you to take a look at the transcript. And what does Mr. Coric's counsel do? She reads out at least half the document before she asks a question. Your Honours, I really don't think that we should go into this any further. I am extremely considerate to what I am saying and toward every other accused, but I appeal to every other -- to all accused to be as patient as General Petkovic for us to deal with all the documents that pertain to him. I do think that this reaction is unfounded. So if you allow me to continue my examination, I will do so, about the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] As I have been mentioned, I would like to say that Ms. Alaburic has forgotten the fact that I haven't yet examined anybody in chief, I have only conducted cross-examination, and in a cross-examination leading questions are allowed. Once we start examining in chief, Ms. Alaburic will be in a position to say how I phrase my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may respond. I haven't mentioned examination-in-chief or cross-examination. I have only referred to the technique of examining a witness; namely, that half a document is read out before a question is put to the witness. So we all know that. No need to waste more time on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's speak about the civilian police, how the civilian police re-subordinated to a military commander. Please take a look at document 3D2408. This is an order --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. I can give -- I can comment. Your Honours, this is an order of the chief of the Department of Interior. He makes use of his authority, and due to the worsening situation in Mostar he orders the civilian police to go to Mostar and be subordinated to the OZ of South-East Herzegovina. And this is a normal procedure on the part of the head of the Department of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who can decide that a unit of the civilian police should be used in combat and, for that purpose, re-subordinated to a military commander?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the head of the Department of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at document P3027. General, I must describe the document for the sake of the transcript. This is an order of the head of the Department of the Interior, dated the 30th of June, 1993. The previous order was not described, so the time reference is lacking from the transcript. That previous document is dated the 9th of May, 1993. That's a reason why documents must be described. Now, General, this one is an order to form a joint police unit. Can you comment on this, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the head of the Department of the Interior, Mr. Kvesic, issued an order on the 30th of June to establish a joint police unit and re-subordinate it to the commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The head of the Department of the Interior, General, did he have the right to take such decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, because they were his units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at document P6027. It is an order issued jointly by the minister of the interior and the minister of defence on the 23rd of October, 1993. Tell us, General, what kind of order is this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the head of the Department of the Interior and the head of the Department of Defence issued a joint command to the effect that for the reinforcement of the HZ-H -- HR-HB forces, the entire reserve police is to be reassigned to the armed forces, whereas the regular units of the police that are on the front-line should be relieved of their duties on the front-line, and that is a regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now the following document in this set, which is P5573. It's a letter sent by the head of the Department of the Interior, dated the 1st of October, 1993, in which in paragraph 5 we can read: "The exclusive right to form these units and make decisions regarding their size, commanding personnel and combat engagement, observing the principles of subordination and command, no one else has the right to render decisions regarding the establishment or combat engagement of police, particularly at a local level." General, is this position of the head of the Department of Defence [as interpreted] a correct rendering of the rules governing the use of police units?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and the head of the Department of the Interior is the only one who has the right to take such decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been entered wrongly in the transcript. On page 43, line 6, the department reads "the Department of Defence," whereas we are speaking about the Department of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the head of the Department of the Interior is in charge of civilian police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak a bit slower and make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we will now deal with the issue of Stupni Do. Unless there are questions about the re-subordination of civilian and military police, I would like to pass on to Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we have prepared a number of documents, but we will be showing only some. But the Trial Chamber has a good overview of the events at Stupni Do. Tell us, General, why did you go to Kiseljak in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there on the occasion of the pulling out of the wounded HVO personnel from that area, and we had to use helicopters to complete that task.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive at Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 17th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How long were you supposed to stay there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 22nd of October, 1993, when I submitted a request to be returned from there by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am looking at the schedule of Petkovic movements that we have, and I cannot help noticing that this does not coincide. I see that you have also noticed. So I just have drawn your attention to it, and I leave it to you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the time being I skipped the topic of the labour of detained persons, because I think due to a shortage of -- the shortage of time, Stupni Do has precedence. But if you will grant me additional time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You may have completely misunderstood me. I was just pointing out that according to this paper that you have presented us, Mr. Petkovic was in Kiseljak from 17 to 26 of October, and you have just said, Mr. Petkovic, that you returned on the 22nd. Which of the two indications is the one that we should base ourselves on?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. If I may just ask for a little bit of patience. General Petkovic said that he was supposed to stay until the 22nd. He didn't say that he really did stay until the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the following document, General, 4D844. Is this the document that you mentioned a short while ago about a flight that you requested to be scheduled for the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I requested to be returned to Herzegovina on the 22nd, and this is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the following document, P6144. This document says that you and Mr. Lucic, as well as Mr. Bandic, stayed at Kiseljak because it was impossible to fly to Split due to adverse weather?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was -- we had bad weather, and the helicopters couldn't take off at Kiseljak to fly to Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, General, how long did you really stay at Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed until the 22nd of -- sorry, 26th of October, 1993, until 9.30 a.m., when I left for Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And with who did you return to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan Bandic, Vinko Lucic, and the driver of Colonel Blaskic. I can't remember his name now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, tell us, when did Ivica Rajic, with some HVO units, set off from Kiseljak to Vares?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivica Rajic left in the night between the 21st and the 22nd of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's see the plans of the ABiH with regard to Vares. Please take a look at document 4D523. It's a document authored by Stjepan Siber, dated the 22nd of October, 1993, in which he replies to the Command of the 3rd Corps. I correct the document reference, which is 4D523, 4D523. And he says, among others -- he was asked about offensive actions in the wider Vares area, and Siber says: "We agree with your proposals with regard to the offensive activities in the area of Vares, the villages of Dragovici and Mijakovici are mentioned, as well as the Plijes facility or building. Tell us, General, in October 1993, while you were at Kiseljak, did you receive information about the ABiH taking these locations mentioned in Siber's letter?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of the places were mentioned. I can see that the village of Kopljari is missing, but Plijes, Dreznica, Borovica, they were taken; and Dragovici and Mijakovici are also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at the following document, General, 4D520. This is an order by Commander Abdulah Ahmic, dated the 23rd of October, 1993, in which he states that combat activities are intensifying, especially in the Stupni Do area, and he goes on to mention help and the unblocking of Stupni Do. And he's also mentioned the Breza MUP intervention unit which shall be kept ready to engage in combat along the axis, et cetera. General, tell us, was there an ABiH unit in the village of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, is the statement in this order true, that on the 23rd of October, combat activities intensified, especially in the Stupni Do area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the following document, 4D519. This is an analysis of the performance or the execution of tasks involved in the Vares operation. It's a document of the 6th Corps of the ABiH. It's a lengthy document, it has about 16 pages. Did you read this analysis, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
