utterances.text: Yes, I read it fully, and it describes who did what in the operation of taking Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what you read in this analysis, does it correspond to the information you have about the events in the Vares municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vares was taken, and everything -- all descriptions of that process matches my information that I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to this analysis, was the operation of taking Vares planned?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation of taking Vares was planned in August 1993, a month and a half after the fall of Kakanj. So Vares was meant to be the next municipality with a majority Croat population that was to be taken by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This analysis speaks about the taking of the Kopljari village, then Plijes, then Lijesnica. The places mentioned, were they taken before Ivica Rajic set off for Vares?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were taken before, and that's why panic broke out in the Command of the Bobovac Brigade, and they requested help from the operations group at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did you agree to the fact that Ivica Rajic, with a number of HVO soldiers, should move to Vares?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the time in Kiseljak, did you agree with Ivica Rajic, what kind of combat activities would be undertaken in the Vares municipality area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was agreed that Ivica Rajic should try and deal with the part of the defence where the BH Army had managed to break through, from the village of Kopljari, towards Mijakovici, along that axis, the western part of the municipality, and to see what the problem of command was there and why a commander was being asking to be relieved of his duties, and to look into the possibility of taking control of that area again or to set up a new line there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, may we go into private session for a few moments, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My question to you, General, is this: This statement made by the witness, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's completely correct, and that's how he acted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is P9954. It is information from Ivica Rajic, dated the 22nd of October, 1993, sent to you, General Petkovic, about the fact that he had arrived in Vares. And my question to you is this: Did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive the information telling me he had arrived in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Apart from this information, did you -- directly from Ivica Rajic in Vares, did you receive any other piece of information in written form, regardless of what the title of that was, while you were in Kiseljak until the 26th of October?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no written information reached me from Ivica Rajic in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us the reason for that. Because we have seen some documents in the courtroom that were addressed to you, among others.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Ivica Rajic realised that on the 22nd I had left Kiseljak, because I said goodbye to him before I left, and I said, I'm going to Herzegovina, and he believed that I had gone to Herzegovina, regardless of the fact that I sent some documents from Kiseljak. He didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is P6026. And it's information from Ivica Rajic, dated the 23rd of October, 1993, and it is addressed, among others, to you, and it is addressed to the chief of staff of the HVO Mostar, Milivoj Petkovic. Tell us, please, General, could this piece of information reach you -- have reached you while you were in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, this piece of information couldn't have reached me, because Paket radio doesn't recognise my name and surname. It only recognises the station to which it is sent, which was Mostar in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. Now let's look at the next document, which is P6028, and that's a document signed by Slobodan Praljak, dated the 23rd of October, about how the problems in Vares should be solved. Tell us, General, did you receive written communication of this type in Kiseljak on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this did reach me late at night in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, what did you think? The calming of the situation in Vares, did that refer to the Muslims or the Croats? How did you understand this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this did not refer to the Muslims. It referred to people in the command and those around the command and headquarters who clashed with the command.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, out of an abundance of caution, I think we should go into private session, because the nature -- in fact, I'd like to go into private session now, before I say anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Let's go into private session, and we'll see whether we have to lift confidentiality or not later on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're obviously on sensitive ground here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, military commanders in Herceg-Bosna, did they have the task and responsibility of investigating crimes and undertaking prosecutions and criminal -- filing criminal reports? Was that their main task?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to have to, at this point, add my voice to that of others. I think there's a very easy way to proceed here, and I know -- I know Ms. Alaburic is concerned about time, but the general is a professional soldier and an educated man. I'm sure if she could just ask, Can you explain the procedures by which these things were done, he could give us an answer in his own words, without being led by a series of "yes" or "no" questions. I think clearly he can be asked, Can you explain to us the disciplinary procedures that a commander would have available to him in these circumstances? And he can give us a narrative response.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have said everything there is to say about disciplinary procedures. And from what we have said so far, you clearly know that the chief of the Main Staff did not have the authority and that officers and non-commissioned officers could not have been punished by a term of imprisonment. I'm just responding to Mr. Scott's comments. Now, Your Honours, if you consider my question to be leading, I will reformulate it and ask it in the following way:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, which organs in Herceg-Bosna were in charge of investigating crimes and prosecuting the perpetrators thereof?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the security services and the crime organs, criminal investigation organs, either attached to the military police or the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, what organs were these? What were they called?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security and Information Service, with its organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Give us the abbreviation of that.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SIS. And the crime departments attached to the military police units and the units attached to the civilian police force, or, rather, the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, repeat that again, because the translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SIS, the Security and Information Service, is the first; and second is the crime Department attached to the military police battalions and the crime departments attached to the Ministry of the -- the Department of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, these crime departments, are they part of the military or civilian police or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one are parts of the civilian police, and the others are part of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, since we've entered into a realm of topics that was not the subject of my examination-in-chief, and my time is short, I now tender a request, along with your interventions, regardless of how long they last, to give me time to the end of today's session, because -- and that might mean half an hour to 40 minutes' additional time, so until the end of business today. May I have that additional time, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So based on the original six hours, you want 20 to 40 additional minutes -- 30 to 40 additional minutes. So in that case, the Prosecutor will also have 6 hours and 40 minutes or 6 hours and 30 minutes. I'll ask my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, if you want an additional 40 minutes, you have them, given that you have actually a credit. So it will be taken off your credit, out of the 55 hours that you had. So there is no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. Thank you. I'd just like to add that not only the Prosecution will have additional time, but the Defence teams, too, just to avoid any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just talk for yourself. Don't deal with the others. I think I'm going to spend another sleepless night. In the meantime, we'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, just two more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I have a question for the Petkovic Defence. When is it going to file its motion for admission of exhibits according to Guide-Line 9?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're working on it, and we'd like to file it on the last day of General Petkovic's testimony. I sincerely hope that we'll manage to do that, but if not, we will file a request to give us about 10 days after the completion of General Petkovic's testimony and certainly not longer than 10 days after the completion of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, just two additional questions, staying with this topic of criminal prosecution. Tell us, in a situation in which a military commander knows that a soldier of his, and knows the first and last name of a soldier, committed a crime, is the military commander duty-bound to file a criminal report to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military commander is duty-bound to file a criminal report with the military prosecutor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's take another situation. A crime has been committed. The perpetrator or perpetrators are unknown, and it is not known whether it is, in fact, a crime that has been committed. Who is going to be responsible for gathering up the information and then possibly file a criminal report with the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two services, the SIS, Security and Information Service, or the military police, so two possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay, General. Now let's return to that Stupni Do of ours and look at P9895, please. Tell us, please, General, have you ever seen this document before? When I say "before," I mean, of course, before these proceedings, so any time before this trial.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean what it says here, "Orders"?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I mean document P9895. It is one word handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two 9895 documents. Do you mean where is says, "Ivica," the text beginning with "Ivica"?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The third page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. But everything is under document P9895. No, I never saw this document before this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in this courtroom, General, it was stated that you dictated these words to Mr. Lucic. Did you dictate anything to anybody, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no need to dictate anything. I'm not incapable of writing four sentences. I'm not lazy, so I would have written them myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, in later communication with Mr. Rajic, did you ever hear any comment of his about this document, or did you hear him question this document at all, ask any questions about it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ivica Rajic never mentioned this document. Ivica Rajic acted as he had been ordered to do and speed up the process of reporting. He didn't refer to any document, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, on the 26th of October, 1993, in the evening, did you happen to talk to Mr. Rajic over the phone?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Praljak explained here in the courtroom that upon my arrival in Kiseljak, I talked to him, and then I carried on my journey to Split. So Rajic couldn't communicate with me, nor did he need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you inform General Praljak, who was your superior officer, about everything you learned about the events at Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we spoke about everything, and I informed him of everything I could and what I knew based on the information that were arriving at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the following document, 4D834.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, the handwritten document that we have, P9895, sent to "Ivica," bearing the name "Petkovic," when reading it any reasonable trier of fact could infer from this --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, every time I'm putting an important question, there is no interpretation. This is really strange. Let me repeat. Can you hear me, General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You all have this document on the screen, and I was saying that any reasonable trier of fact, seeing this document, could infer - could, I say - could infer from it that a person called Petkovic is telling Ivica that the order for an investigation is merely a formality, that he must be cautious, and so forth and so on. So in a nutshell, it means, Don't worry, Ivica. This document is in the hands of the Prosecutor, because there's an ERN number, so I don't know where you found it. Someplace in the archives, probably. But if you gave absolutely no instruction whatsoever, why would this document have been introduced, and why; to your detriment, to harm you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I do not know why this document was introduced. Firstly, we are not duty-bound to give the details about the investigations about (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), and there were three versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I ask to pass into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session. Madam Registrar, could we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On this 8th of November, 1993, where were you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at the command in Citluk, I was in Split, because on the 7th I had a meeting with General Briquemont in Split, and General Praljak testified to that effect. General Praljak received his order on the 8th to take up another position, and he wanted all documents -- all relevant documents, and then Ivica Rajic submitted the first part of a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the second part?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second part arrived, I believe, around the 15th of November, so that the entire report has two parts. This was an amendment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I failed to correct the transcript on page 74, line 25. The general spoke about an investigation conducted by Ivica Rajic, whereas the transcript reads that it was an investigation about Rajic. So just to avoid misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I'll produce only some SIS documents so that we may see whether SIS was up to date with regard to the Stupni Do investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I come back to an answer a short while ago, I seem to see that -- oh, no, I'm sorry. I'm sorry, there was an error in -- I thought I had heard something different. I withdraw. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P6828, it's information from Marijan Biskic. He sent it to the then defence minister, Perica Jukic. We've already looked at this document and it's an exhibit. Remind us, General, if you can, how come Marijan Biskic, the SIS sector in the military police, is writing from the Main Staff of the HVO? How come we have this heading?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan Biskic arrived on the 9th of November. He came to the HVO then. Mr. Biskic still hadn't received an office to work in, nor had he relocated to Mostar. Mr. Biskic was, in fact, in Posusje for most of the time, and probably as he was writing this document in Posusje, he put "Main Staff, HVO, SIS," and "Military Police Sector." And I think a document arrived on which it said -- because the person didn't know, but it had these 12 or 13 people who came to the HVO, so somebody outside the HVO had already written these positions, and the document does not correspond to the actual situation in which Mr. Biskic was at the time. But, anyway, he used the right stamp, the one he had at his disposal, for his use.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, General, which is P6964, which is a piece of information from the head of SIS. And mention is made in this document of the following names: Dominik Ilijasevic, Como; Ante Ljoljo; Marinko Juricic; and so on. Tell us, General, are those the names of the people who are mentioned in other documents as being responsible for the crimes in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, those are the individuals who were in Stupni Do and who were in command of certain groups in the attack on Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document. 4D499 [realtime transcript read in error "4D4999"] is the number. It's a letter from the command or assistant commander for SIS, of the Kiseljak Brigade for SIS. Let me correct the number of the document. It is 4D499. It's a document sent to the District Military Prosecutor's Office in Travnik, telling them that documents are been supplied linked to the investigation at Stupni Do. Now, my question to you, General, is this: Did you know that the Military Prosecutor's Office in Travnik was included in the Stupni Do investigation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that two days after my order. The military prosecutor became involved ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, look at document 4D500 now, please. Is that the document you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is that document. It is the document from the Military Prosecutor's Office, and the date is the 28th of October, 1993, linked to the events in Vares municipality or, rather, Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at a document that comes before this document. It is 4D506. It comes before 4D500. Can you tell us, General, what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from Mr. Perica Jukic, the then defence minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, where he is seeking assistance from UNPROFOR in Kiseljak. He's asking UNPROFOR to send us the information that they have linked to the investigations -- their investigations in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, please, which is P6291. It is a report on the information in Vares which, on the 31st of October, 1993, Ivica Rajic sent to the president of the HZ-HB, that is to say, to Mate Boban. Tell us, General, at the time did you have any knowledge about the direct communication between the supreme commander and Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew about this communication, but we didn't know about this document straight away. We didn't know that Ivica Rajic had compiled a report linked to Stupni Do and addressed to Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, which is P10255. It is a public statement on relieving Ivica Rajic as commander of Operative Group 2. Tell us whether Ivica Rajic was truly relieved of that duty or not.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivica Rajic was not relieved of that duty, and the information was put out by the information media.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us what else important happened with respect to Ivica Rajic giving notice to this position.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it was Mr. Boban's relationship and attitude towards Kiseljak and Kresevo. The Kiseljak and Kresevo municipalities held it against Mr. Boban, because in all the negotiations that were conducted on the organisation of Herceg-Bosna, allegedly, they reproached him for not defending their interests, and never put them in those cantons where there was a Croat majority, but they -- that he allowed them to go -- he allowed Kiseljak and Kresevo to become component parts of provinces with a Croat majority. And that was one of the major complaints by people from Kiseljak. They even threatened that they would rather go with someone else than into the Sarajevo district, and that is why Mate Boban was particularly well disposed towards the Kresevo and Kiseljak municipalities and their leaders, and that's why they had free communication at all times.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But, General, you didn't tell us what important thing happened in respect of Ivica Rajic's de-missioning [sic]. Was he still called "Ivica Rajic"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he changed his name to Viktor Andric a month or so after this date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, Mate Boban, did he know of this name change?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must have known. He certainly did know, because two days later he received a document from Kiseljak where Rajic signed himself as "Viktor Andric."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at P7387, the next document I'd like to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm not sure, but before we leave the page, on line -- page 83, line -- approximately around line 20, 22, it doesn't seem to make sense, the answer there. On the one hand, it says that Mr. Boban would not put Kiseljak and Kresevo in a Croat majority province, but then turns around to say exactly the opposite. I don't know if it's just -- if it was -- someone misspoke or what, but it doesn't seem to make any sense. Perhaps counsel could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, the end of the sentence, where it says that they had free communication throughout, what the did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kiseljak municipality and the leadership of Kiseljak municipality, and Kresevo municipality - they considered themselves to be Croatian municipalities - criticised Mr. Boban for not including them into the Croatian provinces, if I can put it that way. And then from this kind of relationship with them, well, he simply -- he tried to do a service to the Kiseljak people and people in the Kresevo municipality and was constantly in communication with them, promising them that their situation would be improved, that after a certain amount of time that district would be reorganised and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if I understand what you're saying, you mean direct communication between Mate Boban with people from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the communication I meant. Nobody from Central Bosnia had such direct communication with Mate Boban as the military and civilian authorities from Kiseljak enjoyed, and then the people from Kresevo joined in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Still on this point, because I also have a question before you go to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, unless -- and I'm speaking under the control of Mr. Stewart. Unless I have misread or misunderstood, you have told us that (redacted) or something. No -- anyway, he changed it, we know. Now, could you tell us what the procedures are, in the applicable law in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for changing one's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that by law, even today in Croatia and Bosnia, you can go and request a name change, and you can stipulate your reasons. But in this case and at that point in time, (redacted) didn't go that far, although later on he did collect up the necessary documents for (redacted). And later on, some other name, (redacted) or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And was it, to your knowledge, (redacted) -- are we in closed session, actually? We are not. We'll need some redaction. I'm sorry. Was it the person, itself, who decided on the new name that he would bear henceforth, or were any authorities involved by suggestion, assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, I could request a change of my name now, my first and last name. I might choose to be called by some other name. Every person has the right and possibility of asking for a name change, a change in name and surname, at least as far as I know the law and regulations. I think every person is entitled to a name change if they so desire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is actually not the answer to the question that I had intended to put. I don't know whether Ivica Rajic even went to someplace to ask for his name to be changed or whether he simply spread the word, From now on I shall be known under the new name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I know and as far as I was able to learn later from Ivica Rajic's dealings, there was mention of his having -- him having false documents, documents with two names, one in the name of Viktor Andric and the other in the name of Kovac. I think he took another name again. Now, how he came to have official documents in these two names, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I take it that you would say that no one suggested the name change, let alone a specific name. There's two questions, actually. Was it suggested to him that it would be a good idea to change his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not as far as I know, nobody made that suggestion. He made the decision himself. He decided to change his name, and then sent out an information saying that from that day forward, he would be Viktor Andric. And he had a document where it said "Viktor Andric."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Sorry. It is only a very question of detail that -- of course, I do agree with General Petkovic, that most probably the former Yugoslavia, like in Hungary, the changes in names, first name and family name, it is rather often happening, and there is no major problem with this one. I would also add that "Kovac" is a very nice name, too. It is a Hungarian family name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's repeat. Did Mate Boban know about this name change undertaken by Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can assume that he did know, because just a few days after this name change, a letter was sent to Mate Boban with the new name and surname, and I don't think anybody would dare do that unless this person knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at P7387 now, the next document. It's a letter which Viktor Andric, on the 29th of December, 1993, sends to Mate Boban. Now, General, from the contents of the letter, would you say that Mate Boban knew who this man, Viktor Andric, was writing the letter, the writer of the letter?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He most certainly did know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document. It is P7386. Once again, Viktor Andric writing to Mate Boban on the 29th of December. General, from the contents of that letter, could Mate Boban have known for sure who this person, Viktor Andric, was sending him this epistle?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire correspondence was in the name of Viktor Andric from that time on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, we're not going to show the other documents, they're already an exhibit, but tell us, if the person called Viktor Andric, did he have communication with the minister, Lukic [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, with the minister and with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to correct the name in line 17. It's not Lukic, but Jukic with a J.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, General, did you know about this name change, Ivica Rajic's name change?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did learn of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with him, as with Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could move into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness EA --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm done with the Stupni Do chapter. Unless you have additional questions, I would like to go through some of the topics that we had envisaged for the examination-in-chief very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The so-called ultimatum from April 1993, according to all documents that you saw and to the best of your knowledge, did the HVO Main Staff have anything to do with that so-called ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing whatsoever, nor did anybody relate to the Main Staff that there was an ultimatum of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Prozor, in October 1992, how do you see the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH in Prozor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a conflict. We see that as an incident which was over after a day and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did you do during the conflict in Prozor? What were you preoccupied with?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days before that, I started organisational preparations for the Bura operation in the Neretva Valley, and pulled out some materiel from the OZ South-East Herzegovina, among them three Howitzers, and deployed them to the Neretva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf, January 1993. Did you instruct your deputy, Mr. Miro Andric, to go to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was in no position to do so. I was still in Geneva, and I didn't do so from Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you, while Miro Andric was in Gornji Vakuf --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, my apologies. You said that you were in Geneva. I'm interested as to who was in charge of command. How long were you in Geneva for, from which day until which day, because Geneva is not the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, nor is it Croatia, so from which day until which day did you stay in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my first trip there was on the 1st of January, and the conference started on the 2nd. I stayed until the 6th of January, and in the afternoon of that day I returned to Herceg-Bosna. My second trip there was along the following lines: On the 10th, in the morning, I was already at the conference, and on the 12th of January I returned to Zagreb and then continued my voyage to Herzegovina. My third travel there in January 1993 was on the 22nd, in the evening. And on the 23rd, in the morning, the working part of this third conference began. And I returned on the 26th of January, 1993, in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you go back to Geneva in February, March, April, June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. My next trip to Geneva was in late November 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were in Geneva from the 1st -- or the 6th of January -- from the 10th to the 12th of January, 22, 23, and 26th of January. So when you were there, who was in charge of the command of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the first stay, there was Colonel Akrap who stayed there in my stead: On the 7th, Colonel Andric was appointed to the Main Staff. On the 23rd and later, Vukonik [phoen] Andric was on sick leave because he had injured himself, so that this duty was again taken over by Colonel Zeljko Akrap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And from the 10th to the 12th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 10th to the 12th of January, it was Mr. Miro Andric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two minutes before the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, until the end of today's examination or until the end of my examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two minutes left. But in fact you have used 6 hours and 23 minutes, so in fact you have 7 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you grant me 40, it will be 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I asked you whether you gave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I don't think that's a very respectful way of speaking to the Chamber. We have granted you until the end of today, actually. And it would be correct to say that you request that we give you some more. And you simply say, Okay, if you give me 40, then it's 13 more. It's a bit loose. I would suggest that we end the day, because it's been very heavy, and the speed you are keeping is understandable but extremely tiring for us. So I would suggest that you start to continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree fully, and I apologise if I wasn't precise enough and if I wasn't respectful enough. I do apologise if my remark was inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will proceed tomorrow. I'm sure that General Petkovic is also tired, because it's tiring to answer all those questions. And I've been sitting here since 9.00 this morning without a break. So we will all come back here tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00.
